text:
Outside, summer blazed with its torrents of light, with its pyres of
splendor; there in the deep room, behind the closed shutters, behind the
lowered mats, a restful coolness breathed.

Then he took one of her hands and slowly, with a kind of stealth, caressed
it.

“It is strange,” he said, “but you intimidate me. I have always been
somewhat afraid of you. So often I see a kind of mockery on your lips...”

“Really? How odd!”

“Besides, you are right: you must find me almost grotesque. Men in love
are very often ridiculous.”

“And women?” she said.

“Women, I believe, almost never are.”

“What? Grotesque?”

“No, in love.”

“Ah, I could not say... But they certainly confess it less often.”

“Tell me,” he resumed warmly, “tell me that you will come often, that you
will come every day... I want to see you every day! We are so safe here...”

“I am thirsty,” she replied.

Rafa brought her an orangeade so cold that it misted the crystal of the
carafe; then he drank in turn, from the same glass.

“In other years, by this time, I am already in the country,” Rafa said.
“The heat is bad for me. But this year it is impossible for me to leave;
the thought of no longer seeing you is unbearable to me. But what do you
plan to do during the summer?”

“I do not know yet; it does not depend on me.”

“And on whom does it depend?”

“Perhaps on my parents, perhaps...” she added hesitantly, “on my brother.”

“And not on me, in any event?”

“On you? How on you?”

“You once told me, while speaking to me of other things: ‘My family bores
me; perhaps a day will come when I shall be free, entirely free, because
I want to sing.’ Do you remember telling me that?”

“Yes, I remember, and I repeat: A day will come, perhaps soon, when I shall
be free.”

“There, and thinking of that day, I too have had a dream... but one so
beautiful that I do not dare tell it to you.”

“Dreams...” she joked, “dreams have this good thing about them: they serve
to tell things that are too difficult to say.”

“You are right, Loretta,” he admitted. “Then, a dream. That I should get
you a little villa, not too far from Villa Giuliani, small, for you alone.
A secluded little villa, with a lovely garden, an orchard, a stable. You
would be free; no one would know who you were. Sometimes, so as not to
remain alone, you would open the gate for me.”

“Ah... and that is the dream?”

“Yes, that is it.”

She reflected for a moment, then said:

“Go on.”

“What do you mean?”

“After the summer...”

“Well, after the summer you may choose whatever you like. In autumn, for
example, a lovely journey, a little escape, by motorcar, if you wish, even
abroad, if you wish... And in winter, your house in the city, a lady
companion to preserve appearances, a teacher to teach you singing.”

“And in spring,” she exclaimed, still tempted, “as the year blossoms
again, another is put in Lora’s place, and everything begins again: the
same villa, the journey, the house in the city... No, thank you!”

“Another? What are you saying? Have you still not understood that I love
you, that I have loved you for many months, more strongly every day? That
you can make me obey like a child, and that you alone, you alone, must
give me back the peace I no longer have?... Another? That word has no
meaning! Come, reason for a moment. Do you think I do not know what risks
I am running by making you this proposal? Well, what do I care? I do not
want to, I can no longer reflect! No danger frightens me. Only tell me
yes! Ask me for whatever you want, but tell me yes!”

“I am asking for nothing,” she said, regretting that she had allowed
herself to appear so concerned with the future.

“Then listen, hear me...” And he knelt before her armchair and encircled
her with his arms.

“What are you doing? What are you doing?”

“Nothing; I am begging you on my knees. Love me a little, be kind to me
for once!”

Thus on his knees, leaning toward her in the ardor of his desire, with
passionate eyes and a pleading voice, Rafa was almost handsome, and she
looked at him.

“Come, leave me alone...” she said, with a certain annoyance.

He held her tightly around the waist and, bearing down a little against
her, covered her dress and her wrists with tiny kisses.

“How many mistresses have you had sit in this armchair?” she suddenly
asked.

“How many? None.”

“Oh, come now! I am asking you out of curiosity.”

“Perhaps,” he said, “someone has come here, but I do not remember. They
were not mistresses; they were not you. If you do not like it, we shall
change houses. I had no love before knowing you. Now you seem the first
to me. I love you, I love you in every way; you haunt me and I like you.
You are beautiful. You have such an indefinable grace that I suffer when
I am near you. Be kind to me, do not laugh!...”

She was indeed laughing, but with a somewhat nervous laugh, and her mouth,
her eyes, her hands were no longer so calm.

“No, leave me alone...” she pleaded. “Let me go, please... you are hurting
me terribly...”

In the half-light he saw her turn pale; he hid his face in her lap, and
with his arms clasped her knees.

She tried to lift his burning forehead, tried to push away that importunate
mouth, but, unable to overcome his strength, in sudden anger she thrust
her convulsed fingers into his hair.

Then the struggle was brief: in utter abandon, the girl closed her eyes
and let herself be carried away...

But she saw another room, at night, with its windows open above a lake
white with moonlight, and the stars close and infinite; another man bent
over her, covering her with caresses and kisses. And she saw herself
again in that bed, and relived the agony of that lost hour, and for an
instant it seemed to her that he had returned, that he was there, on his
knees, and was kissing her terribly as he had then, and that his hands
were running feverishly, ardently, over all her inflamed body, and that a
mouth was rising, rising to her lips, full of anguish, fever, voluptuousness,
and terror...

A little later, it was dark in the adjoining room, and from room to room,
through the silent house, the cry of her lost virginity was suddenly heard.




II


At about five in the afternoon, Beppe Cianella entered the Club and,
having ordered an iced drink, sprawled indolently on a leather sofa near
the small table where Gigi Saletta, nicknamed Saponetta, and several
others were playing poker.
